In the history of philosophy, the ancient materialists, and all materialists before Marx and Engels, recognized motion as the main property of matter. But in general they reduced every form of motion to a single kind: the mechanical movement of bodies through space, or spatial motion—what Arabic philosophical texts call “motion by transfer.” Because their understanding of motion was so limited, they repeatedly explained motion as the result of an external push. Yet spatial motion is only the lowest and simplest form. From it, motion rises through higher forms: thermal motion, chemical motion, organic living motion, psychological motion, and finally social motion, the highest of these forms. Mechanical motion exists within every one of these higher forms, but the reverse is not true.↩︎
See the French philosopher Dugat, Histoire des philosophes et des théologiens musulmans, Paris, 1878, p. 159.↩︎
Bandali Jawzi, Min Tārīkh al-Ḥarakāt al-Fikriyya fī al-Islām, Dār al-Rawāʾiʿ ed., Beirut, n.d., p. 150.↩︎

This appears in the introduction issued by the Marxist-Leninist Institute, Moscow, Russian ed., 1955, to Engels’s Dialectics of Nature.↩︎

Engels expressed this thesis of Marx in his well-known statement that materialism must change its form with every discovery that marks a new epoch in the natural sciences. See Engels, Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy, in Marx and Engels, Selected Works, Arabic ed., Progress Publishers, Moscow, 1970, vol. 4, p. 29.↩︎
On this point, see Aristotle’s Metaphysics: A, 1, 1199.↩︎

al-Manṣūr was the second Abbasid caliph, ruling from 136 to 158 AH/753–774 CE. He founded Baghdad in 145 AH/762 CE.↩︎

On Arab scientific achievements, see the following: Adam Mez, Die Renaissance des Islams, vol. 2, pp. 1–11, 298–343, 344–362, 363–440; Claude Cahen, Histoire des peuples musulmans, pp. 329–336; de Boer, The History of Philosophy in Islam, pp. 110–115; Rom Landau, Islam and the Arabs, pp. 245–287. One of the best studies of the connection between the development of science among the Arabs and production and social needs is an article by Professor N. Bammate, head of the Division of Philosophical and Humanistic Studies at the University of Paris, titled “The Status of Science and Technology in Islamic Civilization,” published in Philosophy and Culture—East and West, University of Hawaii, Honolulu, 1962, pp. 172–187, in English.↩︎
Rom Landau, Islam and the Arabs, p. 76.↩︎

In Dialectics of Nature, Arabic ed., trans. Usāma al-Qūtlī, Damascus, 1970, Engels says on p. 30 that the Arab discoveries in natural science during the Middle Ages were extremely important, though scattered and for the most part left without further development. On p. 31 he says that a vigorous spirit of free thought grew steadily among the Latin peoples during the European Renaissance, taken over from the Arabs and nourished by Greek philosophy. On p. 34 he says that the Arabs left the European Renaissance decimal notation, the foundations of algebra, modern numerals, and alchemy, while the Christian Middle Ages left nothing.↩︎

In Anti-Dühring, Arabic ed., trans. Fuʾād Ayyūb, Damascus, 1965, p. 27, Engels says that the foundations of exact natural science were first laid by the Greeks in the Alexandrian period and later by the Arabs in the Middle Ages.↩︎
Marx, The Poverty of Philosophy, Arabic trans. André Bazni, Damascus, 1967, 2nd ed., p. 187.↩︎
Lenin, Notebooks on Dialectics, Arabic ed., p. 233.↩︎

On this point, Engels—following Feuerbach—says that it is true that scientific materialism based on natural science forms the foundation of human knowledge, but it is not the whole building. The reason, Engels says, is that we do not live in nature alone; we also live in human society. Society has its own history of development and its own science, just as nature has a history. See Engels, Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy, Arabic ed., p. 30.↩︎
See Engels, Anti-Dühring, Arabic ed., p. 29.↩︎

Among the major scientific events of the nineteenth century that are described as revolutionary changes in the natural sciences, we may mention three examples: 1. the discovery of the cell as the basic unit of bodily structure, which helped establish the idea of development in nature; 2. Darwin’s discovery of the evolution of different biological species; 3. Robert Mayer’s formulation of the theory that different forms of the motion of matter can be transformed into one another. To these we can add Marx’s discovery of the material basis of spiritual life in society, meaning the economy as the foundation of society.↩︎
Engels, Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy, Arabic ed., p. 24.↩︎

For the ancient philosophers and theologians, a thing’s māhiyya, or essence, is its universal reality—the general universal. What refers to the particular, individual thing they call huwiyya, or identity. They also use huwiyya for a thing’s external, material, concrete existence.↩︎
Lenin, Materialism and Empirio-Criticism, Arabic trans. Munīr Shafīq, Damascus, 1971, p. 260.↩︎

Here we limit our discussion to ancient Greek philosophy, not because we regard it as the only source of world philosophy. That would be both historically and methodologically wrong. We do so for two reasons. First, Greek philosophy was the main global source among the sources of Arab philosophy. Second, the ancient Greek philosophers were among the earliest pioneers in forming a view of the unity of existence and nature and in trying to explain the world dialectically, even though from a modern perspective their attempt was spontaneous and naive. This is the point Engels begins from in Dialectics of Nature when he says that almost every type of worldview appears in embryonic form in the different schools of ancient Greek philosophy—in the process of arising and taking shape.↩︎

We should except Pythagoras here, born around 580 or 570 BCE. An early idealist tendency appeared in his well-known idea of “number.” He believed in invisible spirits and emerged as a defender of the ideas of the Greek aristocracy and an opponent of democracy among the slave-owning Greeks.↩︎
See Aristotle, Physics, 203b16, 256b24, and 188a5, Arabic ed., ed. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Badawī, Cairo, 1964, pp. 205, 849, 41.↩︎

We should add that Anaxagoras took an important step forward in addressing the problem of essence. Most of the Ionian philosophers had looked for the source of material things in a single concrete substance, while Empedocles looked for the basis of all existence in four roots, or elements. Anaxagoras then argued that the elements in the material world are infinite and cannot be counted. He also made a brilliant suggestion that points toward recognizing the hand as a basic factor distinguishing human beings from animals.↩︎

We have not included Socrates in this survey because the main task of his philosophy was not to investigate the basic principles of nature or the existence of the world. He limited his philosophy to questions concerning human beings, so it is fair to say that his central philosophical question was: How should a human being live? Socrates’s great contribution, however, was to develop a set of methods of inquiry that later made it possible to overcome the one-sided outlook of the philosophy before him, which had focused on the cosmos and nature while leaving the human being aside.↩︎
See, for example, Plato’s dialogues, especially the Timaeus (27d) and the Theaetetus, in the words of Socrates, together with Plato’s philosophical system as a whole.↩︎
See Aristotle’s criticism of Plato’s Forms in the Metaphysics, 1a and 991a.↩︎

The clearly materialist tendency in Aristotle’s criticism of his teacher Plato, especially at the foundation of the theory of Forms, is what Lenin had in mind when he said that the criticism is directed at idealism as idealism in general, not only at Plato. Lenin wrote this in his notes while summarizing Aristotle’s Metaphysics in the Philosophical Notebooks, and added: “When one idealist criticizes the foundations of idealism in another idealist, materialism gains from it.”↩︎
See Majid Fakhry, Arisṭūṭālīs, Beirut, 1958, p. 33.↩︎

Plotinus states this idea directly in the Fourth Ennead while discussing the nature of the soul: “True existence is the existence of the intelligible world.” See Plotinus, Fourth Ennead, Arabic ed., trans. Fuʾād Zakariyyā, Cairo, 1970, p. 167.↩︎

Aristotle’s demonstrative syllogism is built from three terms: the minor term, the major term, and the middle term. These are arranged into two premises and a conclusion. The two premises must be connected: a major premise, which is a universal proposition, and a minor premise, which is a particular proposition. The minor term appears in the minor premise. Using the traditional example employed by logicians, in the form adopted by Arab philosophers, the syllogism is: Socrates is a human being + every human being is mortal = Socrates is mortal. “Human being” is the middle term, and “Socrates” is the minor term. The first premise in this arrangement—“Socrates is a human being”—is the minor premise, a particular proposition.↩︎

See Professor N. Bammate, “The Status of Science and Technology in Islamic Civilization,” in Philosophy and Culture—East and West, University of Hawaii, Honolulu, 1962, p. 183, in English, while recognizing that the article contains many sound starting points.↩︎
الكتاب: النزعات المادية في الفلسفة العربية - الإسلامية (المجلد الثالث)

إن أحداً من المهتمين بالشأن الثقافي لا يجهل الأهمية الفكرية التاريخية لصدور كتاب العلامة الشهيد حسين مروة «النزعات المادية في الفلسفة العربية - الإسلامية»، ولا يجهل الفراغ الذي سده الكتاب، الذي أراده كاتبه موسوعياً، في المكتبة العربية، وبشكل خاص المكتبة الديمقراطية والتقدمية، والمكتبات الفردية للمثقفين بشكل عام وللتقدميين منهم خاصة، هذا عدا طلاب الجامعات وكافة المهتمين بالشأن الثقافي العام.

ولكن الذي حدث أن الكتاب الضخم قد صدر عن دارنا «دار الفارابي» في مجلدين فقط بلغ أولهما أكثر من ألف صفحة في حين بلغ الثاني حوالي ثمانمائة صفحة. وهكذا توالت طبعات الكتاب واحدة تلو الأخرى، حتى أصبح الكتاب مرجعاً أساسياً للمثقفين والباحثين في الجامعات العربية وطلبتها الذين نجد بينهم اليوم من هو مهتم بالجاهلية مثلاً دون غيرها أو بالمنهجية فقط، أو يهتم بالتحليل المادي لفلسفة ابن سينا بصرف النظر عن الأقسام الأخرى. هذا عدا كون شراء قسم من الكتاب يكلف القارئ أقل من سعر الكتاب كله.
